# Part A: Adult acquired flatfoot (progressive collapsing foot deformity)

## 1. Terminology and anatomy
- **Adult acquired flatfoot deformity (AAFD)**, renamed **progressive collapsing foot deformity (PCFD)** (2020 consensus): **complex 3D deformity** with **hindfoot valgus, forefoot abduction (talonavicular uncoverage), forefoot varus (supination), medial column instability (collapse of the arch)**, and later **ankle valgus**.
- **Tibialis posterior (TP):** **strongest invertor; primary dynamic stabiliser of the medial longitudinal arch**; inserts mainly on the **navicular tuberosity** with slips to the cuneiforms, cuboid and metatarsal bases 2-4; **locks the transverse tarsal (Chopart) joint** (TN and CC axes become non-parallel: rigid lever for push-off); **antagonist: peroneus brevis**.
- **Hypovascular zone** of TP tendon: **behind and just distal to the medial malleolus** (degeneration site).
- **Static stabilisers:** **spring ligament (calcaneonavicular: superomedial part most important)**, **deltoid ligament (deep)**, **plantar fascia (windlass mechanism)**, **talocalcaneal interosseous ligament**.
- **Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction (PTTD)** was the classic cause, but **spring ligament failure** is now recognised as central; TP failure is often secondary.

## 2. Causes
- **TP tendon degeneration (commonest in middle-aged obese women; hypertension, diabetes, steroid injections, seronegative arthropathy)**.
- **Others:** **inflammatory arthritis (RA)**, **trauma (TP laceration/rupture, Lisfranc injury)**, **neuropathic (Charcot)**, **tarsal coalition (adult presentation)**, **accessory navicular**, **degenerative TMT/naviculocuneiform arthritis**, **iatrogenic**.

## 3. Clinical evaluation
- **Medial ankle pain along the TP tendon** (early), **lateral sinus tarsi/subfibular impingement pain** (late: calcaneofibular impingement).
- **"Too many toes" sign** (**forefoot abduction seen from behind**).
- **Single-limb heel rise test**: **inability to perform / no heel inversion on heel rise** (**most sensitive test for TP dysfunction**); **double heel rise** to check flexibility (hindfoot inverts if flexible).
- **Flexibility of the hindfoot (subtalar)** and **forefoot (forefoot varus/supination: compensatory fixed or flexible)**: **assess forefoot position with the hindfoot held in neutral**.
- **Gastrocnemius/Achilles contracture** (**Silfverskiöld test**: almost universal).
- **Medial column instability** (first TMT/naviculocuneiform plantar sag), **deltoid laxity (ankle valgus)**.

## 4. Imaging
- **Weight-bearing radiographs (AP and lateral foot, AP ankle, hindfoot alignment view (Saltzman))**:
  - **Lateral talo-first metatarsal angle (Meary angle): normal 0 degrees (collinear)**; **over 4 degrees convex plantar = flatfoot** (**mild 4-15, moderate 15-30, severe over 30**),
  - **Calcaneal pitch angle (normal about 20-30 degrees; reduced in flatfoot)**,
  - **AP talonavicular coverage angle (over 7 degrees) / talonavicular uncoverage percentage (over 40%)**: forefoot abduction,
  - **AP talo-first metatarsal angle** (**abduction**),
  - **Medial cuneiform-floor height** (reduced), **sinus tarsi impingement**, **subfibular impingement**.
  - **Ankle: talar tilt (valgus) in the mortise** (deltoid failure).
- **Weight-bearing CT** (**3D, subfibular impingement, middle facet subluxation**: **peritalar subluxation**).
- **MRI** (TP tendon tears/tendinosis, spring ligament), **ultrasound**.

## 5. Classification
### Johnson and Strom (modified by Myerson/Bluman)
| Stage | TP tendon | Hindfoot | Treatment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **I** | **Tenosynovitis/tendinosis; normal length** | **Normal alignment; can single heel rise** (painful) | **Non-operative (immobilisation, NSAIDs, orthoses)**; **tenosynovectomy** |
| **II** (A/B/C) | **Elongated/dysfunctional** | **Flexible flatfoot** (**IIA mild abduction; IIB abduction over 30-40% TN uncoverage; IIC fixed forefoot varus**) | **Joint-sparing reconstruction**: **FDL transfer to the navicular + medializing calcaneal osteotomy (MDCO) ± lateral column lengthening (Evans) ± Cotton osteotomy ± gastrocnemius recession ± spring ligament repair** |
| **III** | **Ruptured/degenerated** | **Rigid flatfoot (fixed hindfoot valgus)** | **Triple arthrodesis** (or **double/modified: TN + subtalar**) |
| **IV** (A/B) | | **+ ankle valgus (deltoid failure)**: **IVA flexible (correctable), IVB rigid (tibiotalar arthritis)** | **IVA: deltoid reconstruction + hindfoot correction**; **IVB: tibiotalocalcaneal (TTC) or pantalar arthrodesis, or TAR + hindfoot correction** |
### PCFD consensus classification (2020)
- **Stage 1 (flexible) or 2 (rigid)**, with **classes A (hindfoot valgus), B (midfoot/forefoot abduction), C (forefoot varus/medial column instability), D (peritalar subluxation/dislocation), E (ankle instability: valgus)**; each scored as flexible or rigid.

## 6. Treatment details
- **Non-operative (all stages first, mainstay in elderly/low demand):** **CAM boot or short leg cast (acute tenosynovitis, 4-8 weeks)**, **orthoses (medial arch support + medial heel wedge; UCBL)**, **ankle-foot orthosis (Arizona brace)** for later stages, **physiotherapy (eccentric TP strengthening, Achilles stretching)**, weight loss. **Avoid steroid injection into the TP tendon sheath (rupture)**.
- **Flexible deformity (stage II) procedures:**
  - **FDL transfer to the navicular** (**FDL is in phase with and adjacent to the TP; weaker (about 30%) but adequate when combined with bony correction**; **FHL** alternative; **interconnection (Henry knot) allows the FHL to flex lesser toes**),
  - **Medializing displacement calcaneal osteotomy (MDCO)** (**about 10 mm medial shift**: **converts the Achilles tendon pull into an invertor (medial to the subtalar axis)**; **protects the tendon transfer**; **sural nerve and lateral calcaneal branch at risk; the tibial nerve/tarsal tunnel at risk with large shifts**),
  - **Lateral column lengthening (Evans osteotomy: anterior calcaneus between the anterior and middle facets, about 10-15 mm from the CC joint; or CC distraction arthrodesis)** for **forefoot abduction (TN uncoverage over about 40%)**: **lateral column overload (lateral foot pain: commonest complication)**, **CC arthritis**, **sural nerve injury**, non-union,
  - **Cotton osteotomy (plantarflexion opening-wedge osteotomy of the medial cuneiform)** or **first TMT arthrodesis (Lapidus)** for **residual forefoot varus/medial column instability**,
  - **Spring ligament repair/reconstruction**,
  - **Gastrocnemius recession (Strayer) / Achilles lengthening (Hoke)** for equinus,
  - **Subtalar arthroereisis** (sinus tarsi implant: limited role in adults; mainly paediatric).
- **Rigid deformity (stage III):** **triple arthrodesis (subtalar, TN, CC)** through **medial and lateral incisions (or single medial incision: protects lateral skin)**; **TN joint is the key joint (fusion of TN alone eliminates almost all hindfoot motion)**; **position: hindfoot about 5 degrees valgus, neutral forefoot rotation (plantigrade), neutral abduction**; **complications: non-union (TN commonest site), malunion, adjacent joint arthritis (ankle, naviculocuneiform)**.
- **Stage IV:** **deltoid ligament reconstruction** (flexible) or **TTC/pantalar arthrodesis** (rigid with arthritis); **total ankle replacement with hindfoot realignment**.

# Part B: Pes cavus

## 7. Definition and causes
- **Elevated medial longitudinal arch (high arch), often with hindfoot varus**; **forefoot-driven (plantarflexed first ray) or hindfoot-driven**.
- **About two-thirds have an underlying neurological cause**: **Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (HMSN type I: commonest; autosomal dominant; PMP22 duplication on chromosome 17p)**, **spinal cord pathology (tethered cord, diastematomyelia, syringomyelia, tumour, spinal dysraphism)**, **cerebral palsy**, **poliomyelitis (India: residual polio)**, **Friedreich ataxia**, **stroke**, **muscular dystrophy**. **Also:** **idiopathic/familial (subtle cavovarus)**, **residual clubfoot**, **trauma (compartment syndrome: Volkmann's ischaemic contracture: claw toes; malunited talar neck fracture)**.
- **Unilateral cavus = spinal cord lesion until proved otherwise: MRI whole spine.** **Bilateral cavus: think CMT (nerve conduction studies, genetic testing)**.

## 8. CMT pathomechanics
- **Muscle imbalance (pairs of agonist/antagonist; weakest muscles first: tibialis anterior and peroneus brevis; intrinsics):**
  - **Weak tibialis anterior vs strong peroneus longus**: **plantarflexed first ray (forefoot pronation/valgus)**,
  - **Weak peroneus brevis vs strong tibialis posterior**: **hindfoot varus, forefoot adduction**,
  - **Intrinsic weakness**: **claw toes** (**EDL recruited to dorsiflex the ankle: hyperextends MTPJs**),
  - **Plantar fascia contracture** (windlass: elevates the arch).
- **Tripod effect**: **plantarflexed first ray forces the hindfoot into varus on weight bearing (forefoot-driven hindfoot varus)**.
- **Lateral ankle instability, peroneal tendon tears, fifth metatarsal stress fractures, lateral foot callosities, stress fractures, ankle arthritis (varus)**.

## 9. Evaluation
- **Peek-a-boo heel sign** (**medial heel pad visible from the front with the feet parallel: hindfoot varus**).
- **Coleman block test** (**block under the lateral foot (heel and lateral forefoot), allowing the first ray to drop off the edge**): **hindfoot varus corrects = flexible hindfoot, deformity is forefoot-driven** (treat the forefoot: **first metatarsal dorsiflexion osteotomy + plantar fascia release**); **does not correct = fixed hindfoot varus (needs calcaneal osteotomy or arthrodesis)**.
- **Muscle power testing** (MRC grading of each muscle: guides tendon transfers), **neurological examination** (reflexes, sensation, spine), **calluses (under first and fifth metatarsal heads)**.
- **Radiographs:** **Meary angle (talo-first metatarsal) convex dorsally (negative: over -4 degrees = cavus)**, **calcaneal pitch angle increased (over 30 degrees: calcaneocavus)**, **Hibbs angle** (calcaneus axis vs first metatarsal axis: **under 150 degrees** = cavus), **"double talar dome"** (ankle AP/lateral: hindfoot varus/external rotation), **fibula posterior**.

## 10. Treatment
- **Non-operative:** **orthoses (lateral forefoot post + recess under the first metatarsal head)**, **lateral heel wedge** (for flexible hindfoot), **AFO** (foot drop), **physiotherapy**, **footwear**.
- **Operative (individualised; "flexible deformities need soft-tissue/tendon procedures, fixed deformities need bony procedures, arthrodesis for severe rigid deformity or arthritis"):**
  - **Soft tissue:** **plantar fascia release (Steindler)**, **gastrocnemius recession/Achilles lengthening** (**in calcaneocavus (polio/spina bifida) the Achilles is weak: do not lengthen**).
  - **Tendon transfers (balance forces):** **peroneus longus to peroneus brevis transfer** (**removes plantarflexion of the first ray; augments eversion**), **tibialis posterior transfer to the dorsum (through the interosseous membrane to the lateral cuneiform)** for **foot drop**, **Jones transfer (EHL to the first metatarsal neck + hallux IPJ fusion)** for **clawed hallux**, **Hibbs transfer (EDL to the lateral cuneiform/cuboid)** for **claw lesser toes**, **flexor-to-extensor transfer (Girdlestone-Taylor)** for flexible claw toes.
  - **Bony (joint-sparing):** **dorsiflexion closing-wedge osteotomy of the first metatarsal base** (**forefoot-driven cavus**), **lateral closing-wedge calcaneal osteotomy (Dwyer)** or **lateralising calcaneal (Z) osteotomy** (**fixed hindfoot varus**), **midfoot osteotomy (Cole: dorsal closing wedge through the navicular-cuneiform/cuboid; Japas V-osteotomy; Akron dome)** for **midfoot cavus**, **anterior tibial osteotomy** rarely.
  - **Arthrodesis:** **triple arthrodesis** (**rigid deformity, arthritis, salvage**; **worse long-term results in CMT (ankle/midfoot arthritis)**: **avoid when possible in young patients**).
  - **Lateral ankle ligament reconstruction** (Broström) **must be combined with correction of the varus** (otherwise fails).

## 11. Paediatric flatfoot (brief link)
- **Flexible flatfoot: physiological; no treatment unless painful + tight heel cord (calcaneal lengthening + gastrocnemius recession)**.
- **Rigid flatfoot: tarsal coalition, CVT, accessory navicular, inflammatory, neuromuscular**: see paediatric foot notes.

## 12. Other conditions
- **Tibialis anterior tendon rupture:** **elderly men (sixth-seventh decade)**, **degenerative**, **foot slap/steppage gait**, **palpable gap/mass at the anterior ankle**, **EHL/EDL substitution (toe clawing on dorsiflexion)**; **repair/reconstruction (EHL transfer, graft) in active patients**; **AFO in low-demand**.
- **Accessory navicular (os naviculare)** in adults: **Kidner procedure (excision + TP advancement)**.
- **Tarsal tunnel syndrome:** **tibial nerve compression beneath the flexor retinaculum (laciniate ligament)**; **space-occupying lesions (ganglion, varicosities, lipoma, accessory muscles: flexor digitorum accessorius longus)**, **hindfoot valgus (traction)**, trauma; **burning plantar paraesthesia (sparing the heel (calcaneal branch arises proximal) in some cases), Tinel sign, dorsiflexion-eversion test**; **NCS**; **MRI**; **decompression (release of the flexor retinaculum + abductor hallucis fascia (medial and lateral plantar nerve tunnels))**: **results less predictable than CTS (about 50-75%)**, best with a **space-occupying lesion**.
- **Baxter nerve (first branch of the lateral plantar nerve / inferior calcaneal nerve) entrapment**: **chronic heel pain (medial)** mimicking plantar fasciitis; **abductor digiti minimi atrophy on MRI**; decompression with plantar fascia release.
- **Plantar fasciitis (heel pain):** **degenerative fasciosis at the medial calcaneal tubercle origin**; **first-step morning pain (post-static dyskinesia)**; **calcaneal spur (in FDB origin) is incidental**; **non-operative (about 90%: plantar fascia-specific stretching (best), Achilles stretching, heel cups, night splints, NSAIDs)**; **steroid injection (risk of fat pad atrophy and plantar fascia rupture)**, **ESWT**; **surgery (partial plantar fascia release (medial third to half: avoid complete release: lateral column overload)** ± **Baxter nerve release, gastrocnemius recession)** after **6-12 months**.

> Exam pearl: **PCFD/AAFD: TP + spring ligament failure; too many toes; can't single-heel-rise (most sensitive). Johnson-Strom: I tendinosis (conservative), II flexible (FDL transfer + MDCO ± Evans ± Cotton ± gastroc recession), III rigid (triple arthrodesis), IV ankle valgus (deltoid recon or TTC/TAR). MDCO converts Achilles to an invertor; Evans = lateral column overload.**

> Exam pearl: **Meary angle: plantar convex = flatfoot, dorsal convex = cavus. Calcaneal pitch high = calcaneocavus. TN joint key to triple arthrodesis (TN non-union commonest); position 5 degrees valgus.**

> Exam pearl: **Cavus: unilateral = spinal MRI; bilateral = CMT (PMP22). CMT: weak TA vs strong PL (plantarflexed first ray), weak PB vs strong TP (varus). Coleman block: corrects = forefoot-driven (first MT dorsiflexion osteotomy + plantar fascia release + PL to PB); does not correct = add Dwyer/lateralising calcaneal osteotomy. Jones transfer for clawed hallux. Broström fails without varus correction.**

> Exam pearl: **Tarsal tunnel: flexor retinaculum, space-occupying lesion gives best release results. Plantar fasciitis: stretching best; partial release only. Baxter nerve: ADM atrophy.**

# Part A: Hallux valgus

## 1. Definition and aetiology
- **Lateral deviation of the hallux at the first MTPJ with medial deviation of the first metatarsal (metatarsus primus varus)**, with a medial prominence ("bunion").
- **Women (about 10:1 in surgical series)**, **familial (about 60-90% of juvenile cases; maternal transmission)**, **constricting footwear (narrow toe box, high heels)**, **ligamentous laxity**, **pes planus**, **first ray hypermobility (debated)**, **long first metatarsal**, **rounded metatarsal head**, **increased DMAA**, **inflammatory arthritis (RA)**, **neuromuscular (cerebral palsy, stroke)**, **amputation of the second toe**.

## 2. Pathoanatomy (sequence)
1. **Medial capsule and medial sesamoid ligament attenuation**; **the hallux drifts laterally (valgus)** pulled by **adductor hallucis** and the lateral pull of the **EHL and FHL** (**bowstring effect: become deforming forces**).
2. **The metatarsal head drifts medially off the sesamoids** (the **sesamoids stay in place: anchored by the adductor hallucis and the transverse metatarsal ligament**): **apparent lateral sesamoid displacement** relative to the metatarsal head; **crista erosion**.
3. **Pronation (eversion) of the hallux** (abductor hallucis migrates plantarly: loses abduction power; becomes a flexor/pronator).
4. **Lateral capsule and adductor contracture**; **transfer metatarsalgia** under the second metatarsal head (first ray loses load-bearing).
5. **Second toe deformities** (crossover toe, hammer toe), **second MTPJ instability/plantar plate tear**.

## 3. Evaluation
- **Weight-bearing AP and lateral radiographs** (and sesamoid axial view).
- **Normal values and severity:**
| Angle | Normal | Mild | Moderate | Severe |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Hallux valgus angle (HVA: first MT axis vs proximal phalanx axis)** | **Under 15 degrees** | **15-20** (up to 20-25 in some schemes) | **20-40** | **Over 40** |
| **Intermetatarsal angle (IMA: 1st-2nd MT)** | **Under 9 degrees** | **9-11** (under 13) | **11-16** (13-20) | **Over 16** (over 20) |
| **Distal metatarsal articular angle (DMAA)** | **Under 10 degrees** (about 6-10) | | | |
| **Hallux valgus interphalangeus (HVI)** | **Under 10 degrees** | | | |
- **Congruent vs incongruent joint:** **congruent (articular surfaces parallel; increased DMAA; juvenile)** vs **incongruent (subluxed: lateral subluxation of the phalanx on the head)**. **Congruent deformity: correction must not be done by soft-tissue release alone (would create an incongruent joint): use DMAA-correcting osteotomy (biplanar chevron) or extra-articular (double/triple) osteotomies**.
- **Sesamoid position (Hardy and Clapham: grades 1-7)**, **first MTPJ arthritis** (**hallux rigidus: fusion instead**), **first TMT hypermobility** (**dorsal translation over about 8-10 mm: Lapidus**), **metatarsus adductus** (**increased difficulty; IMA underestimated**), **pronation of the first metatarsal (round lateral head sign)**.

## 4. Management
### Non-operative
- **Wide toe-box footwear, bunion pads, orthoses, toe spacers**; **do not correct the deformity**; **surgery is for pain, not cosmesis** ("**never operate for cosmesis**").
### Operative principles: choose by severity, joint congruency, arthritis and TMT stability
| Deformity | Procedure | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Mild (HVA under 30, IMA under 13), congruent or incongruent** | **Distal metatarsal osteotomy: Chevron (Austin)** (**V-shaped osteotomy at the metatarsal head, apex distal; lateral shift up to about 30-50% of the head width**) ± **distal soft-tissue procedure (lateral release)** | **AVN of the metatarsal head** (**lateral release + chevron: avoid excessive dorsolateral dissection: nutrient vessels enter dorsolaterally (first dorsal metatarsal artery) and plantar-laterally**); **biplanar chevron for increased DMAA** |
| **Moderate (HVA 30-40, IMA 13-20)** | **Scarf osteotomy** (**Z-shaped diaphyseal osteotomy**: lateral translation; **troughing (fragments telescope into each other: elevation of the head, loss of height)**), **proximal metatarsal osteotomy (proximal chevron, crescentic, opening/closing wedge, Ludloff, Mau)** + **distal soft-tissue release** (modified McBride) | **Proximal osteotomies: more powerful correction (each degree of correction at the base produces more displacement distally)**; **dorsal malunion (elevatus: transfer metatarsalgia)** |
| **Severe (HVA over 40, IMA over 20)** | **Proximal osteotomy + distal soft-tissue procedure**, **Lapidus (first TMT arthrodesis)** | |
| **First TMT hypermobility / generalised laxity / recurrent HV** | **Modified Lapidus (first TMT arthrodesis)** | **Non-union (about 5-10%)**, **shortening (transfer metatarsalgia)**, dorsiflexion malunion |
| **Arthritis of the first MTPJ, severe deformity, neuromuscular, RA, salvage of failed surgery** | **First MTPJ arthrodesis** | **Position: about 10-15 degrees valgus, about 10-15 degrees dorsiflexion relative to the floor (about 20-25 degrees relative to the first metatarsal shaft), neutral rotation**; **IMA corrects spontaneously** after fusion |
| **Hallux valgus interphalangeus** | **Akin osteotomy** (**medial closing-wedge osteotomy of the proximal phalanx**) | Adjunct to other osteotomies |
| **Elderly, low-demand** | **Keller resection arthroplasty** (**excision of the base of the proximal phalanx**) | **Cock-up deformity, transfer metatarsalgia, weakness of push-off**; largely abandoned |
| **Juvenile/adolescent** | **Delay until skeletal maturity** (**high recurrence**); **guided growth (lateral hemiepiphysiodesis of the first metatarsal)** | **Increased DMAA common** |
- **Simple bunionectomy (Silver) alone**: **high recurrence; not used alone**.
- **McBride procedure** (original): **excision of the lateral sesamoid** (**hallux varus risk**), **adductor tenotomy**, **medial capsulorrhaphy**: **modified McBride = lateral release without sesamoid excision**.
- **Minimally invasive (MIS) third/fourth generation (MICA/percutaneous chevron-Akin)**: increasingly used; similar outcomes; learning curve.

## 5. Complications
- **Recurrence (commonest; about 10-25%)**: **undercorrection of the IMA**, **unrecognised increased DMAA**, **unaddressed pronation**, **first TMT hypermobility**, **juvenile**, **poor sesamoid reduction**.
- **Hallux varus** (**overcorrection: excessive lateral release, lateral sesamoid excision, excessive medial eminence resection (staking the sagittal sulcus), overtightened medial capsule, IMA overcorrection (negative)**): **flexible: EHB tenodesis/EHL transfer; rigid/arthritic: MTPJ fusion**.
- **AVN of the metatarsal head** (**chevron + extensive lateral release**).
- **Transfer metatarsalgia** (**shortening or dorsal malunion of the first metatarsal**).
- **Stiffness of the first MTPJ**, **non-union/malunion**, **infection**, **dorsomedial cutaneous nerve injury (neuroma)** (**medial dorsal cutaneous branch of the superficial peroneal nerve**), **CRPS**.

# Part B: Hallux rigidus

## 6. Hallux rigidus (first MTPJ OA)
- **Commonest arthritis of the foot**; **dorsal osteophyte (dorsal bunion)** limiting **dorsiflexion (pain at push-off)**; **positive grind test (late)**; **adolescent form (OCD of the metatarsal head)**.
- **Coughlin and Shurnas classification (grades 0-4):** **0 stiffness, normal radiograph**; **1 mild, dorsal osteophyte, preserved joint space**; **2 moderate, joint space narrowing, pain at extremes**; **3 severe, under 10-20% residual motion, pain at extremes, more narrowing**; **4: as 3 with pain in mid-range (positive grind test)**.
- **Treatment:**
  - **Non-operative:** **stiff-soled shoe, rocker sole, Morton's extension (carbon plate)**, NSAIDs, steroid injection.
  - **Cheilectomy** (**excision of the dorsal osteophyte and dorsal 25-30% of the metatarsal head**): **grades 1-2 (and selected 3)**; **pain at the extremes, not mid-range**; **± Moberg osteotomy (dorsal closing-wedge osteotomy of the proximal phalanx: shifts the arc into dorsiflexion)**.
  - **First MTPJ arthrodesis**: **gold standard for grades 3-4** (**predictable pain relief**; **position: 10-15 degrees dorsiflexion relative to the floor, 10-15 degrees valgus, neutral rotation**).
  - **Interpositional arthroplasty/Keller** (elderly), **hemiarthroplasty (synthetic cartilage implant, Cartiva: mixed results)**; **silicone/total joint arthroplasty: high failure (silicone synovitis, subsidence)**.

# Part C: Lesser toe deformities and forefoot pain

## 7. Lesser toe deformities
| Deformity | MTPJ | PIPJ | DIPJ | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Mallet toe** | Neutral | Neutral | **Flexed** | **FDL contracture** |
| **Hammer toe** | **Neutral or slightly extended** | **Flexed** | **Neutral/extended** | **Commonest; second toe**; FDL/FDB contracture |
| **Claw toe** | **Hyperextended** | **Flexed** | **Flexed** | **Usually multiple toes, bilateral: neuromuscular (CMT, diabetes neuropathy), RA, cavus foot**: **intrinsic weakness** (lumbrical/interossei) |
| **Curly toe** | | Flexed + varus (rotated) | | **Congenital** (FDL tightness) |
- **Flexible deformities: flexor-to-extensor transfer (Girdlestone-Taylor: FDL split to the extensor hood/dorsum of the proximal phalanx)**, **FDL tenotomy (mallet)**.
- **Fixed deformities: PIPJ resection arthroplasty (DuVries) or PIPJ arthrodesis**; **MTPJ: extensor tendon lengthening (EDL Z-lengthening), EDB tenotomy, dorsal capsulotomy**; **Weil osteotomy** (**oblique shortening osteotomy of the metatarsal neck**: for **MTPJ dislocation/subluxation, long metatarsal**: **floating toe** = commonest complication).
- **Crossover second toe / second MTPJ instability (plantar plate tear):** **dorsomedial drift of the second toe**, **pain under the second MTPJ**, **positive drawer (Lachman) test of the MTPJ**; **Coughlin plantar plate grading**; **plantar plate repair + Weil osteotomy**, flexor-to-extensor transfer.
- **Freiberg disease** (second metatarsal head osteochondrosis: adolescent girls; dorsal closing-wedge osteotomy).

## 8. Metatarsalgia
- **Pain under the metatarsal heads**: **primary** (**long second metatarsal**, plantarflexed metatarsal, **cavus foot**, prominent condyles), **secondary** (**inflammatory arthritis, Freiberg, MTPJ synovitis, gastrocnemius tightness**), **iatrogenic (transfer after hallux valgus surgery)**.
- **Intractable plantar keratosis (IPK)**: **discrete** (beneath a prominent fibular condyle) vs **diffuse** (beneath a long metatarsal).
- **Gastrocnemius contracture (positive Silfverskiöld test: ankle dorsiflexion limited with the knee extended, improves with the knee flexed)**: **gastrocnemius recession (Strayer)**.
- **Treatment:** **metatarsal pad (placed proximal to the metatarsal heads)**, rocker-bottom sole, orthoses; **Weil osteotomy**, **condylectomy**.

## 9. Morton neuroma (interdigital neuroma)
- **Perineural fibrosis of the common digital nerve** (**not a true neuroma**), **distal to the deep transverse metatarsal ligament**; **third web space (between 3rd and 4th metatarsal heads) commonest**, then second; **women (about 5-10:1)**, **narrow/high-heeled shoes**.
- **Burning plantar forefoot pain radiating into the toes**, **numbness**, **"walking on a pebble"**; **Mulder click (squeezing the forefoot mediolaterally while pressing the web space)**, **web space tenderness**; **splaying of the toes (Sullivan sign)**.
- **Imaging: ultrasound or MRI** (size **over about 5 mm**); **differentials: MTPJ synovitis/plantar plate tear (second web), stress fracture, intermetatarsal bursitis, tarsal tunnel syndrome, lumbar radiculopathy**.
- **Treatment:** **wide shoes, metatarsal pad, steroid injection (up to about 50-80% relief)**, **alcohol sclerosing injections**, **radiofrequency ablation**; **surgery: neurectomy (dorsal approach preferred: avoids plantar scar; divide the deep transverse metatarsal ligament; resect the nerve proximal to the ligament, about 3 cm)** (**about 80-90% success**); **recurrent (stump) neuroma (about 5-10%)**: **plantar approach** for revision; **decompression (ligament release) alone** as an alternative.

## 10. Sesamoid disorders
- **Sesamoiditis, stress fracture, AVN, osteochondritis, OA, bipartite sesamoid (medial/tibial sesamoid commonest: about 10-30%; bilateral in about 85%: compare with the other foot)**, **turf toe**.
- **Turf toe:** **hyperdorsiflexion injury of the first MTPJ (plantar plate/capsuloligamentous complex)**: **American football on artificial turf**; **grade I** sprain, **II** partial tear, **III** complete tear (**proximal migration of sesamoids**, **sesamoid diastasis**, **vertical instability: Lachman positive**); **grade III: surgical repair** of the plantar plate.
- **Treatment of sesamoid pain:** offloading (dancer's pad, orthoses), boot/cast; **sesamoidectomy** (refractory: **excision of both sesamoids causes cock-up deformity: avoid**; **medial sesamoid excision: hallux valgus**; **lateral sesamoid excision: hallux varus**).

## 11. Bunionette (tailor's bunion)
- **Lateral prominence of the fifth metatarsal head**; **Coughlin types:** **I enlarged/prominent head**, **II lateral bowing of the fifth metatarsal**, **III increased 4-5 intermetatarsal angle (over 8-10 degrees: commonest symptomatic)**.
- **Treatment:** **wide shoes**; **type I: lateral condylectomy** or **distal chevron osteotomy**; **type II: distal chevron or diaphyseal (oblique/scarf) osteotomy**; **type III: diaphyseal oblique or proximal osteotomy** (**proximal fifth metatarsal osteotomy: poor blood supply: non-union**).

> Exam pearl: **HVA under 15 and IMA under 9 normal; DMAA under 10. Sesamoids stay; the metatarsal head drifts medially. Congruent joint (increased DMAA, juvenile) needs DMAA-correcting osteotomy, not soft-tissue release. Mild: chevron; moderate: scarf/proximal osteotomy; severe/hypermobile: Lapidus; arthritic: fusion (10-15 valgus, 10-15 dorsiflexion to floor). Commonest complication: recurrence; hallux varus = overcorrection (lateral sesamoid excision).**

> Exam pearl: **Hallux rigidus: Coughlin-Shurnas; cheilectomy for pain at the extremes (grade 1-2, ± Moberg); mid-range pain/grind (3-4) = fusion.**

> Exam pearl: **Claw toe (MTPJ hyperextension): neuromuscular/cavus; flexible: Girdlestone-Taylor (FDL to extensor). Crossover second toe = plantar plate tear (drawer test): repair + Weil (floating toe). Morton neuroma: 3rd web, Mulder click, distal to DTML; neurectomy via dorsal approach. Bunionette type III (increased 4-5 IMA) = diaphyseal osteotomy.**

# Part A: Achilles tendon

## 1. Anatomy
- **Formed by the gastrocnemius (medial and lateral heads: cross the knee) and soleus** (± plantaris medially); **largest and strongest tendon in the body** (loads up to **about 12 times body weight** in running).
- **Fibres rotate about 90 degrees** (medial fibres become posterior, **soleus fibres insert medially**) as they descend: stress concentration.
- **Paratenon** (no true synovial sheath), **insertion on the middle third of the posterior calcaneal tuberosity** (footprint); **retrocalcaneal bursa** (between tendon and calcaneus) and **retro-Achilles (subcutaneous) bursa**.
- **Blood supply:** **posterior tibial artery (proximal and distal)**, **peroneal artery (mid-portion)**; **hypovascular watershed zone about 2-6 cm proximal to the insertion** (**site of most ruptures and mid-portion tendinopathy**).
- **Sural nerve**: crosses from medial to lateral, **lateral to the tendon at about 10 cm proximal to the insertion** (**at risk in lateral incisions and percutaneous repairs**).

## 2. Acute Achilles tendon rupture
- **Epidemiology:** **men aged 30-50 ("weekend warriors")**, **sudden eccentric loading** (push-off with knee extended, unexpected dorsiflexion), **left more than right**; **2-6 cm above the insertion (commonest)**.
- **Risk factors:** **fluoroquinolones**, **corticosteroids (systemic or local injection)**, **pre-existing tendinopathy**, inflammatory arthritis, gout, **renal failure, hyperparathyroidism**, previous contralateral rupture.
- **Clinical:** **"kicked in the back of the leg"**, **audible pop**, **weak plantarflexion (but often preserved through FHL, FDL, TP, peronei)**: **missed in about 20%**.
  - **Simmonds-Thompson test (calf squeeze: absent plantarflexion = rupture)** (**most reliable**),
  - **Palpable gap**,
  - **Matles test** (**loss of resting plantarflexion tension: the injured foot hangs in neutral/dorsiflexion with knees flexed prone**),
  - **Increased passive dorsiflexion**, **O'Brien needle test**, **Copeland sphygmomanometer test**.
  - **Two of the clinical tests (AAOS guideline) sufficient for diagnosis.**
- **Imaging:** **ultrasound** (gap, **gap distance in plantarflexion (over 5-10 mm)**: may guide treatment); **MRI** (chronic/equivocal); **radiograph: Kager's fat pad distortion (triangle obscured), avulsion fracture (calcaneal tuberosity avulsion: "beak" fracture: urgent surgery: skin necrosis)**.

### Management
| | **Non-operative (functional rehabilitation)** | **Operative (open or minimally invasive)** |
|---|---|---|
| Re-rupture | **About 3-12% (similar to surgery when early functional rehab is used)** | **About 2-5%** |
| Complications | Re-rupture; **tendon elongation (weaker push-off)** | **Wound complications/infection (about 5-10% open), sural nerve injury (percutaneous: about 5-10%)**, DVT |
| Strength | Possibly slightly weaker (elongation) | Slightly better plantarflexion strength in some studies |
- **Evidence:** **early functional rehabilitation (early weight bearing in an equinus boot with heel wedges)** reduces the re-rupture difference: **Willits (2010)**, **UKSTAR trial (2020, UK: functional bracing vs plaster casting: similar outcomes)**, **Scandinavian trials (Nilsson-Helander, Ochen meta-analysis)**: **surgery reduces re-rupture absolute risk by about 2-3% at the cost of more complications**; **choice individualised** (**athletes, delayed presentation, large gap, avulsion: surgery**).
- **Non-operative protocol:** **equinus (about 20-30 degrees plantarflexion) in a boot with wedges**, **early protected weight bearing (2 weeks)**, **gradual reduction of equinus over 6-8 weeks**, **avoid passive dorsiflexion stretching for 12 weeks**; return to sport about 6-9 months.
- **Operative:** **open repair (Krackow/Bunnell core sutures + epitendinous; medial incision avoids the sural nerve)**, **minimally invasive/percutaneous (Achillon, PARS, Ma-Griffith)** (**fewer wound problems, sural nerve risk**); **repair with the ankle in resting tension (compare with the contralateral side)**.
- **Calcaneal tuberosity (sleeve) avulsion fracture: urgent ORIF (skin at risk)**.

## 3. Chronic (neglected) Achilles rupture
- **Over 4-6 weeks**; **gap with scar**; **weak push-off, inability to single heel rise**, **increased passive dorsiflexion**.
- **Kuwada classification** (gap): **I partial**, **II complete with gap under 3 cm (end-to-end repair)**, **III gap 3-6 cm (V-Y advancement / gastrocnemius recession / tendon graft)**, **IV gap over 6 cm (tendon transfer + graft)**.
- **Myerson:** **under 1-2 cm: end-to-end repair**; **2-5 cm: V-Y lengthening (gastrocnemius aponeurosis) ± FHL transfer**; **over 5 cm: FHL transfer (± turndown flap, allograft)**.
- **FHL transfer** (**strongest, in phase, adjacent, vascularised muscle belly brings blood supply, low donor morbidity**) to the calcaneus (**tunnel**); **FDL, peroneus brevis** alternatives; **gastrocnemius turndown flap (Bosworth/Lindholm)**.

## 4. Achilles tendinopathy
| | **Mid-portion (non-insertional)** | **Insertional** |
|---|---|---|
| Location | **2-6 cm proximal to the insertion** | **At the calcaneal insertion** |
| Patients | **Runners, active middle-aged** | **Older, less active, overweight**, inflammatory arthritis (seronegative) |
| Pathology | **Tendinosis (degeneration, neovascularisation)**, **paratenonitis** (crepitus, fixed tender area) | **Calcification/enthesophyte (spur)**, **Haglund deformity (posterosuperior calcaneal prominence)**, **retrocalcaneal bursitis** |
| Signs | **Painful fusiform swelling that moves with the tendon (painful arc sign)**; **Royal London Hospital test** | **Posterior heel tenderness, bump ("pump bump")** |
| First-line | **Eccentric loading (Alfredson protocol: 3 x 15 reps, twice daily, 12 weeks, knee straight and bent)** or **heavy slow resistance**; **ESWT**; **high-volume injection**, sclerotherapy | **Eccentric loading on flat ground (not into dorsiflexion)**, **heel lift**, **shoe modification (open-backed)**, **ESWT** |
| Surgery (after 6 months) | **Debridement/longitudinal tenotomies**, **stripping of paratenon/neovessels**, **plantaris release (medial)**, **gastrocnemius recession**, **FHL transfer if over 50% of tendon debrided** | **Haglund resection + debridement of calcification + reattachment (suture anchors)** (**central tendon-splitting approach**); **FHL transfer** for extensive degeneration (over 50%); **Zadek (dorsal closing-wedge calcaneal) osteotomy** |
- **Haglund syndrome:** **Haglund deformity + retrocalcaneal bursitis + insertional tendinopathy**; **radiographic: Fowler-Philip angle (over 75 degrees)**, **parallel pitch lines (Pavlov)**.
- **Avoid steroid injections into the Achilles** (rupture); **fluoroquinolones** caution.

# Part B: Other tendons

## 5. Peroneal tendons
- **Anatomy:** **peroneus brevis (anterior/medial, closer to the fibula, in the retromalleolar groove; inserts on the base of the fifth metatarsal)**, **peroneus longus (posterior/lateral; crosses under the cuboid in the cuboid tunnel to insert on the base of the first metatarsal and medial cuneiform)**; **superior peroneal retinaculum (SPR: from the posterolateral fibula to the calcaneus)**; **fibrocartilaginous rim** deepens the groove; **os peroneum** (sesamoid in PL at the cuboid: about 20%).
- **Peroneus brevis split tears:** **longitudinal splits from compression against the fibula** (**cavovarus foot, ankle instability, low-lying PB muscle belly, peroneus quartus**): **lateral ankle pain/swelling**; **MRI ("boomerang/chevron" shape)**; **debridement and tubularisation (if under 50% involved)**, **tenodesis to PL (if over 50%)**; **correct cavovarus**.
- **Peroneal tendon subluxation/dislocation:** **forceful dorsiflexion with peroneal contraction (skiing)**; **SPR avulsion with a "fleck sign" (rim fracture of the lateral malleolus: Eckert-Davis grade 3)**; **Eckert-Davis/Oden grades (1: SPR stripped from the fibula with periosteum (commonest); 2: fibrocartilaginous rim elevated with SPR; 3: bony avulsion; 4: SPR torn from calcaneal attachment)**. **Acute: cast trial (about 50% success) or SPR repair**; **chronic: SPR repair/reconstruction + fibular groove deepening**. **Intrasheath subluxation** (tendons swap position within the groove).
- **Painful os peroneum syndrome (POPS):** **PL rupture at the cuboid notch/os peroneum fracture**; **proximal migration of the os peroneum on serial radiographs = PL rupture**; excision + PB tenodesis.

## 6. Tibialis posterior
- See flatfoot notes (PCFD).

## 7. Flexor hallucis longus
- **FHL tenosynovitis ("dancer's tendinitis")**: **ballet dancers (en pointe)**: **posteromedial ankle pain, triggering of the hallux ("hallux saltans")**, **pain on resisted hallux flexion**; **stenosis at the fibro-osseous tunnel behind the talus (between the medial and lateral talar tubercles)**; associated with **posterior ankle impingement (os trigonum/Stieda process)**: **rest, physiotherapy; release of the FHL tunnel ± os trigonum excision (open posteromedial or arthroscopic/endoscopic posterior)**.
- **Knot of Henry**: FHL-FDL crossover (plantar midfoot).

## 8. Tibialis anterior
- **Rupture: elderly men, degenerative**; see flatfoot notes.

## 9. Posterior ankle impingement
- **Os trigonum** (**unfused lateral tubercle of the posterior talar process: about 7-14%**) or **Stieda process** (elongated lateral tubercle); **ballet dancers, footballers (forced plantarflexion: nutcracker)**; **posterior ankle pain in plantarflexion (forced plantarflexion test)**, **diagnostic injection**; **excision (posterior arthroscopy: posterolateral and posteromedial portals with the patient prone; FHL is the landmark: stay lateral to FHL to protect the tibial neurovascular bundle)**.
- **Anterior ankle impingement:** **"footballer's ankle"**: **anterior tibial and talar neck osteophytes (kissing)** (**bony**) or **anterolateral soft-tissue impingement (Bassett ligament: accessory anteroinferior tibiofibular ligament fascicle; meniscoid lesion (Wolin))**; **arthroscopic debridement**; **anterior arthroscopy portals: anteromedial (medial to the tibialis anterior) and anterolateral (lateral to peroneus tertius: superficial peroneal nerve (intermediate dorsal cutaneous branch) at risk: commonest complication of ankle arthroscopy)**; **avoid the anterocentral portal (dorsalis pedis/deep peroneal nerve)**.

## 10. Plantar fascia rupture
- **Acute rupture** (often after steroid injection), **plantar heel pain and bruising**; non-operative (boot).

## 11. Gastrocnemius-soleus problems
- **Tennis leg** (**medial head of gastrocnemius tear at the musculotendinous junction**; middle-aged; "shot in the calf"); **differentiate from DVT (ultrasound)**; non-operative.
- **Isolated gastrocnemius contracture** (**Silfverskiöld test**): associated with **metatarsalgia, plantar fasciitis, Achilles tendinopathy, PCFD, midfoot arthritis**: **gastrocnemius recession (Strayer: distal aponeurosis; Baumann: intramuscular proximal)** (**sural nerve at risk**); **Achilles lengthening (Hoke triple hemisection: percutaneous)** when both gastrocnemius and soleus are tight (**overlengthening: calcaneal gait/weak push-off**).

> Exam pearl: **Achilles: watershed 2-6 cm above insertion; sural nerve lateral at about 10 cm. Thompson test most reliable. Early functional rehab narrows re-rupture difference (UKSTAR, Willits); surgery: fewer re-ruptures, more wound/sural complications. Chronic gap over 5 cm: FHL transfer (± V-Y/turndown).**

> Exam pearl: **Mid-portion tendinopathy: eccentric Alfredson (12 weeks), plantaris release. Insertional: no dorsiflexion eccentrics; Haglund resection + debridement + reattachment; FHL if over 50% debrided. Avoid steroid injections and fluoroquinolones.**

> Exam pearl: **Peroneus brevis split tears (cavovarus): under 50% repair, over 50% tenodesis to PL. Peroneal dislocation: SPR, fleck sign; groove deepening for chronic. Os peroneum migration = PL rupture. Dancers: FHL tendinitis + os trigonum (stay lateral to FHL arthroscopically). Ankle arthroscopy: anterolateral portal risks the superficial peroneal nerve.**

# Part A: Ankle instability

## 1. Lateral ligament complex
- **Anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL):** **weakest and most commonly injured**; **intracapsular**; **taut in plantarflexion** (resists **anterior translation and inversion in plantarflexion**); from the anterior fibula about **1 cm proximal to the tip** to the talar neck/body.
- **Calcaneofibular ligament (CFL):** **extracapsular**, **deep to the peroneal tendons (floor of the peroneal sheath)**; **taut in dorsiflexion**; resists **inversion in neutral/dorsiflexion**; **crosses both the ankle and subtalar joints**.
- **Posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL):** strongest; **rarely injured** (only in dislocations).
- **Injury sequence (inversion in plantarflexion): ATFL first, then CFL, then PTFL.**

## 2. Acute lateral ankle sprain
- **Commonest sports injury**; **inversion + plantarflexion**.
- **Grading:** **I** stretch, **II** partial tear (ATFL torn), **III** complete tear (ATFL + CFL).
- **Ottawa ankle rules (radiograph if):** **pain in the malleolar zone AND** (**bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus (distal 6 cm)**, or **inability to bear weight (4 steps) immediately and in the emergency department**); **foot: navicular or base of 5th metatarsal tenderness** (**sensitivity close to 100%**; reduce radiographs by about 30-40%).
- **Examination (delayed 4-5 days improves accuracy):** **anterior drawer test** (**ATFL**; **over 10 mm absolute or over 3-5 mm side-to-side difference = abnormal**), **talar tilt test** (**CFL**; **over 10-15 degrees or over 5 degrees side-to-side**).
- **Differential diagnosis/associated injuries:** **high ankle (syndesmotic) sprain**, **osteochondral lesion of the talus (OLT)**, **peroneal tendon injury**, **fractures: lateral process of the talus ("snowboarder's fracture"), anterior process of the calcaneus, base of the 5th metatarsal, os trigonum**, **Maisonneuve**, **deltoid injury**, **subtalar instability**.
- **Treatment:** **functional treatment** (**brief protection (brace/boot for severe), early mobilisation, proprioceptive and peroneal strengthening**) **is superior to immobilisation** for most; **grade III: short below-knee cast/boot (about 10 days) improves early outcomes (Lamb, CAST trial)**; **acute surgical repair rarely indicated** (elite athletes debatable).
- **Chronic symptoms after sprains in about 20-40%** (pain, instability).

## 3. Chronic lateral ankle instability
- **Mechanical instability** (**pathological laxity: positive drawer/tilt**) vs **functional instability** (**subjective giving way: proprioceptive deficit, peroneal weakness**).
- **Evaluate:** **hindfoot alignment (cavovarus: Coleman block test)**, **generalised laxity (Beighton)**, **peroneal tendons (split tears)**, **OLT**, **anterior impingement**, **subtalar instability**, **syndesmosis**.
- **Imaging:** **stress radiographs** (**anterior drawer: over 10 mm absolute or 3 mm side-to-side; talar tilt over 10 degrees or 5 degrees side-to-side**), **MRI** (associated lesions), **ultrasound**.
- **Non-operative first:** **peroneal strengthening and proprioceptive (balance board) rehabilitation for at least 3-6 months**, braces.
- **Surgery:**
  - **Anatomic repair: modified Broström-Gould procedure (gold standard)** (**imbrication/shortening of the ATFL and CFL + reinforcement with the inferior extensor retinaculum (Gould modification)**): **about 85-95% good results**; **arthroscopic Broström** increasingly used.
  - **Augmentation (suture tape/internal brace)** for poor tissue, hyperlaxity, high-demand.
  - **Anatomic reconstruction with free tendon graft (gracilis/semitendinosus/allograft)**: **failed Broström, poor-quality tissue, generalised laxity (Ehlers-Danlos), heavy patients, long-standing instability**.
  - **Non-anatomic tenodeses (peroneus brevis): Watson-Jones, Evans, Chrisman-Snook**: **historical**: **restrict subtalar motion, stiffness, sacrifice of PB**.
  - **Correct cavovarus (lateralising calcaneal osteotomy, first metatarsal dorsiflexion osteotomy)** if present: **otherwise failure**.
  - **Concomitant ankle arthroscopy** for intra-articular lesions (OLT, impingement).
- **Complications:** **superficial peroneal nerve injury (commonest)**, **sural nerve injury**, **stiffness (loss of inversion)**, recurrence.

## 4. Syndesmotic (high ankle) sprains
- **External rotation + dorsiflexion**: **AITFL (first), interosseous ligament, PITFL, transverse ligament**; **collision sports**; **longer recovery (about 2x lateral sprains)**.
- **Tests:** **squeeze test (Hopkin)**, **external rotation stress test (Kleiger: most sensitive)**, **crossed-leg test**, **Cotton test (lateral translation of the talus)**, **fibular translation test**.
- **Radiographs (weight-bearing/stress):** **tibiofibular clear space over 6 mm (1 cm above the plafond on AP and mortise: most reliable)**, **tibiofibular overlap under 6 mm on AP (or under 1 mm on mortise)**, **medial clear space over 4-5 mm (deltoid injury)**; **bilateral weight-bearing CT** (subtle diastasis), **MRI**; **arthroscopy (gold standard: over 2 mm diastasis on probing)**.
- **Treatment:** **stable (no diastasis): non-operative (boot, protected weight bearing)**; **unstable/diastasis: fixation (syndesmotic screws (3.5-4.5 mm, 1-2 screws, 3-4 cortices, about 2-5 cm above the plafond, angled 20-30 degrees anteriorly from posterior) or suture-button devices (dynamic; fewer removals, better reduction))**; **anatomic reduction of the fibula in the incisura is the key (malreduction = poor outcome)**; **direct visualisation/CT** recommended.
- **Chronic syndesmotic instability:** debridement + fixation/reconstruction; **arthrodesis** of the syndesmosis (salvage).

## 5. Medial (deltoid) ligament injury and instability
- **Superficial deltoid** (tibiospring, tibionavicular, tibiocalcaneal: **resists hindfoot eversion**) and **deep deltoid (anterior and posterior tibiotalar: primary restraint to lateral talar shift and external rotation)**.
- **Isolated deltoid injuries are rare** (usually with **fractures (bimalleolar equivalent)** or syndesmotic injury); **chronic medial instability** associated with **PCFD (stage IV)** and valgus ankles.
- **Gravity stress test / external rotation stress test**: **medial clear space over 4-5 mm** (or **over 1 mm greater than the superior clear space**) = deep deltoid insufficiency.
- **Repair/reconstruction (anatomic, anchors, graft)**.

## 6. Subtalar instability
- Often **coexists with lateral ankle instability (CFL, cervical and interosseous talocalcaneal ligaments)**; difficult to diagnose (**Brodén stress views**); **reconstruct the CFL** (anatomic reconstruction addressing both joints).

# Part B: Ankle arthritis

## 7. Epidemiology and aetiology
- **Post-traumatic (about 70-80%: rotational ankle fractures, pilon fractures, recurrent instability)**, **primary OA (uncommon: about 10%)**, **inflammatory (RA)**, **haemophilia**, **neuropathic (Charcot)**, **AVN of the talus**, **septic sequelae**, **varus/valgus malalignment (cavovarus, PCFD)**.
- **Ankle cartilage is thinner (about 1-1.7 mm) but more resistant to OA** than the knee (**higher proteoglycan content, stiffer, less response to catabolic cytokines (IL-1), smaller contact area but high congruency**): **younger patients (post-traumatic) than hip/knee OA**; **disability comparable to end-stage hip OA or heart failure (SF-36)**.

## 8. Evaluation
- **Weight-bearing AP, mortise and lateral ankle + foot radiographs**, **hindfoot alignment view (Saltzman)**, **long-leg alignment**; **weight-bearing CT**.
- **Classifications:** **Takakura (varus OA: stage 1 sclerosis/osteophytes, 2 medial narrowing, 3A medial gutter obliteration, 3B narrowing to the talar dome, 4 whole joint)**; **Kellgren-Lawrence**; **COFAS** (for TAR planning).
- **Assess:** **coronal deformity (varus/valgus: congruent vs incongruent)**, **ligament stability**, **hindfoot/subtalar arthritis**, **bone stock**, **soft tissues**, **vascular status**, **neuropathy**, **adjacent joint arthritis**, **smoking**, **infection history**.

## 9. Non-operative treatment
- **Activity modification, weight loss, NSAIDs, bracing (lace-up brace, AFO (Arizona)), rocker-bottom sole with SACH heel (solid ankle cushioned heel)**, **intra-articular steroid/hyaluronic acid (limited evidence)**, PRP (experimental).

## 10. Joint-preserving surgery
- **Arthroscopic debridement (anterior impingement osteophytes)**: **for impingement symptoms with preserved joint space**; poor for diffuse arthritis.
- **Supramalleolar osteotomy (SMOT):**
  - **Indication:** **asymmetric (varus or valgus) ankle OA with partially preserved (at least 50%) joint surface** (**Takakura 2-3A**), **younger patients**.
  - **Medial opening-wedge (or lateral closing-wedge) tibial osteotomy for varus OA** (**overcorrect slightly to about 2-4 degrees valgus**) ± **fibular osteotomy**; **medial closing-wedge for valgus OA**.
  - **Contraindications:** **end-stage panarthritis**, **severe hindfoot instability**, **neuropathy**, **inflammatory arthritis**, **severe talar tilt (incongruent joint with over about 10 degrees tilt: relative)**.
  - **Delays fusion/TAR** (about 10 years in many patients).
- **Distraction arthroplasty (circular frame distraction 5 mm for about 3 months)**: **young patients**; cartilage repair; variable results.
- **Osteochondral allograft (total ankle allograft)**: high failure; limited role.

## 11. Ankle arthrodesis
- **Gold standard for end-stage ankle arthritis** (especially **young, heavy laborers, infection history, neuropathy, severe deformity, poor bone stock (talus), failed TAR**).
- **Position: neutral dorsiflexion (90 degrees), 5 degrees hindfoot valgus, external rotation about 5-10 degrees (equal to the contralateral foot), talus translated slightly posteriorly (decreases lever arm/knee hyperextension)**; **equinus position = genu recurvatum/knee pain; varus = lateral foot overload**.
- **Techniques:** **arthroscopic arthrodesis** (**faster union (about 8-12 weeks), lower complications, less blood loss** in mild deformity: **under about 10-15 degrees**), **open (anterior or transfibular lateral approach)** for deformity/bone loss; **fixation: 2-3 crossed cannulated cancellous screws (6.5-7.3 mm)** ("**home-run screw**" from the posterior malleolus into the talar neck), **anterior plates**, **TTC nail (when subtalar also fused)**.
- **Union rate about 85-95%**; **non-union about 5-15%** (**smoking (strongest modifiable risk), diabetes, AVN of the talus, open approach, infection, previous fracture**).
- **Long-term: adjacent joint arthritis (subtalar about 50-100% radiographically, talonavicular, midfoot) at about 7-20 years**; gait: **reduced sagittal motion compensated by midfoot (about 30% of ankle motion remains through adjacent joints)**; **shoe wear: rocker sole**.
- **Fusion takedown/conversion to TAR** for painful adjacent joint disease (selected).

## 12. Total ankle replacement (TAR)
- **Modern designs: 2-component (fixed-bearing: INBONE, Infinity, STAR (US: some versions), Salto Talaris)** and **3-component (mobile-bearing: STAR (Europe), Hintegra, Mobility (withdrawn), BOX)**.
- **Indications:** **older (over about 50-55), lower-demand patients with end-stage OA**, **bilateral ankle arthritis**, **adjacent hindfoot/midfoot arthritis or fusion (TAR preserves motion: protects adjacent joints)**, **inflammatory arthritis**, **good bone stock and soft tissues**, **correctable deformity (under about 10-15 degrees coronal; up to 20 degrees with adjunctive procedures)**.
- **Contraindications:** **active or recent infection**, **Charcot neuroarthropathy/neuropathy**, **AVN of the talus (large)**, **severe PAD**, **severe uncorrectable deformity/instability**, **poor soft-tissue envelope**, **young heavy labourers (relative)**, **non-reconstructable ligaments**, **paralysis**.
- **Outcomes:** **survivorship about 70-90% at 10 years** (registry: **revision rates higher than hip/knee arthroplasty**); **functional outcomes comparable to arthrodesis (TARVA trial, UK 2022: similar AOFAS/MOXFQ at 1 year; TAR slightly better in some subgroups)**; **better gait, preserved motion, less adjacent joint degeneration**, but **more reoperations**.
- **Complications:** **wound complications (commonest; anterior approach: about 5-15%; thin skin)**, **intraoperative malleolar fracture (medial malleolus)**, **aseptic loosening/subsidence (talar component commonest)**, **periprosthetic osteolysis/cysts**, **gutter impingement (medial/lateral; heterotopic ossification)**, **polyethylene wear/fracture**, **infection**, **nerve injury (superficial and deep peroneal)**, **edge loading (malalignment)**.
- **Failed TAR:** **revision TAR (custom/stemmed talar components)** or **conversion to arthrodesis (TTC nail with bulk allograft (femoral head): "salvage arthrodesis")**: **union rates lower (about 80%)**.
- **Adjunctive procedures to balance the TAR:** **deltoid release (varus)**, **lateral ligament reconstruction**, **calcaneal osteotomy**, **subtalar/TN fusion**, **gastrocnemius recession**, **SMOT** (staged).

## 13. Osteochondral lesions of the talus (OLT) (link)
- **Medial (posteromedial: deeper, cup-shaped, often atraumatic: commonest location)** and **lateral (anterolateral: shallow, wafer-like, traumatic)**.
- **Berndt and Harty (radiographic: I compression, II partial detachment, III complete detachment, non-displaced, IV displaced fragment)**, **Hepple (MRI)**, **Ferkel (CT)**.
- **Treatment:** **non-operative (3-6 months) for non-displaced**; **arthroscopic debridement + bone marrow stimulation (microfracture)** for **lesions under about 1-1.5 cm² (or under 15 mm diameter)**; **fixation of large acute fragments**; **osteochondral autograft (OATS from the knee) or allograft**, **ACI/MACI** for **large (over 1.5 cm²) or cystic lesions or failed microfracture**; **medial malleolar osteotomy** for posteromedial access (**malunion/non-union risk**).

> Exam pearl: **ATFL weakest, taut in plantarflexion, intracapsular, injured first; CFL extracapsular, under the peroneals, taut in dorsiflexion, crosses ankle and subtalar joints. Ottawa rules: malleolar bone tenderness at posterior edge/tip of distal 6 cm or can't bear weight 4 steps.**

> Exam pearl: **Chronic instability: rehab 3-6 months first; modified Broström-Gould (inferior extensor retinaculum) gold standard; correct cavovarus (else failure); superficial peroneal nerve commonest nerve injury. Syndesmosis: clear space over 6 mm (most reliable), ER stress test most sensitive; anatomic fibular reduction; suture button vs screw.**

> Exam pearl: **Ankle OA mostly post-traumatic. Asymmetric OA with over 50% joint preserved = SMOT. Arthrodesis position: neutral, 5 valgus, 5-10 ER, posterior talus; smoking = non-union; adjacent subtalar arthritis long-term. TAR: older, bilateral, adjacent fusion, inflammatory; contraindicated in infection, Charcot, talar AVN; wound problems commonest; TARVA similar to fusion.**

diabetic foot and Charcot.md:
# Part A: The diabetic foot

## 1. Epidemiology and pathogenesis
- **Lifetime risk of foot ulceration in diabetes: about 15-25%**; **about 85% of diabetic lower-limb amputations are preceded by an ulcer**; **5-year mortality after major amputation is about 50-70%** (worse than many cancers). **India has one of the largest diabetic populations** (barefoot walking, late presentation, infection).
- **Triad:**
  1. **Peripheral neuropathy (commonest underlying cause of ulcers; about 80-90%)**:
     - **Sensory** (loss of protective sensation: **10-g Semmes-Weinstein monofilament**: **inability to feel it = loss of protective sensation**; **128 Hz tuning fork (vibration)**, **ankle reflexes**, **biothesiometer (VPT over 25 V)**),
     - **Motor** (intrinsic weakness: **claw toes, prominent metatarsal heads, fat pad displacement**: high plantar pressures),
     - **Autonomic** (**dry, cracked skin (anhidrosis)**, **arteriovenous shunting: warm foot with bounding pulses**, increased bone blood flow: osteopenia).
  2. **Peripheral arterial disease (PAD)**: **infrapopliteal (tibial/peroneal) arteries**, **foot arteries often spared**; **medial arterial calcification (Mönckeberg sclerosis) makes ABI falsely high (over 1.3: non-compressible)**: **use toe pressures (over 30-40 mmHg needed for healing), toe-brachial index (TBI under 0.7 abnormal), transcutaneous oxygen pressure (TcPO2 over 30-40 mmHg predicts healing)**, **arterial Doppler waveforms**, **angiography**.
  3. **Infection** (impaired immunity: neutrophil dysfunction with hyperglycaemia).
- **Other factors:** **deformity** (hallux valgus, claw toes, Charcot), **limited joint mobility (glycosylation of collagen: stiff joints, Achilles contracture: forefoot pressure)**, **previous ulcer/amputation (strongest predictor of new ulcer)**, poor glycaemic control, **renal failure (dialysis)**, smoking, poor footwear, visual impairment.

## 2. Classification of ulcers
### Wagner (Meggitt-Wagner) classification
| Grade | Description |
|---|---|
| **0** | **Intact skin (pre-ulcerative lesion, deformity, healed ulcer)** |
| **1** | **Superficial ulcer (skin and subcutaneous)** |
| **2** | **Deep ulcer to tendon, capsule or bone (no abscess/osteomyelitis)** |
| **3** | **Deep ulcer with abscess, osteomyelitis or septic arthritis** |
| **4** | **Localised (forefoot/toe) gangrene** |
| **5** | **Whole-foot gangrene** |
- **Limitation:** **does not account for ischaemia or infection separately**.
### University of Texas (UT) classification
- **Grade (depth): 0 pre/post-ulcerative, 1 superficial, 2 to tendon/capsule, 3 to bone/joint**, **Stage: A clean, B infected, C ischaemic, D infected and ischaemic** (**stage predicts amputation better than grade**).
### Other
- **SINBAD** (Site, Ischaemia, Neuropathy, Bacterial infection, Area, Depth: **IWGDF recommended for communication**), **WIfI** (**Wound, Ischaemia, foot Infection**: **SVS, predicts amputation risk and benefit of revascularisation**), **PEDIS** (IWGDF infection classification: perfusion, extent, depth, infection, sensation).
- **IWGDF/IDSA infection severity:** **uninfected**, **mild (local, cellulitis under 2 cm)**, **moderate (cellulitis over 2 cm or deeper tissue: abscess, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, fasciitis)**, **severe (SIRS/systemic toxicity)**.

## 3. Assessment of the ulcer
- **Probe-to-bone test** (**sterile metal probe touching bone**): **high positive predictive value for osteomyelitis in high-prevalence settings** (and high negative predictive value in low-prevalence settings).
- **Radiographs** (**osteomyelitis changes appear after 10-14 days: periosteal reaction, cortical erosion, osteolysis**; gas in soft tissue; foreign bodies), **MRI (most sensitive and specific imaging for osteomyelitis: marrow oedema on T1 hypointense (confluent low T1 signal is the most specific), T2/STIR hyperintense; sinus tracts, abscesses)**, **labelled leucocyte scan/PET-CT** (when MRI contraindicated; helps differentiate Charcot from osteomyelitis).
- **Bone biopsy (histology + culture): gold standard for osteomyelitis diagnosis** (percutaneous through intact skin, or at surgery); **superficial swab cultures are unreliable** (deep tissue samples after debridement).
- **Inflammatory markers: ESR over 70 mm/h suggests osteomyelitis**; CRP, procalcitonin.
- **Organisms:**
  - **Mild/acute infections: aerobic gram-positive cocci (*S. aureus*, beta-haemolytic streptococci)**,
  - **Chronic/previously treated/severe: polymicrobial (gram-negatives: *Pseudomonas* (macerated wounds), Enterobacteriaceae; anaerobes (necrosis/ischaemia)), MRSA**.

## 4. Management principles
- **Multidisciplinary diabetic foot team** (**reduces major amputation rates by about 40-80%**): diabetologist, orthopaedic/vascular surgeon, podiatrist, orthotist, wound nurse, microbiologist.
- **Offloading (the cornerstone for neuropathic plantar ulcers):**
  - **Total contact cast (TCC): gold standard** (**forces compliance: non-removable**; **contraindicated with infection, ischaemia, deep/draining wounds**; change weekly; **healing about 80-90% in 6-8 weeks**),
  - **Non-removable knee-high walker ("instant TCC")** (**equivalent**), removable walkers (compliance issues), **felted foam**, therapeutic footwear.
- **Debridement** (**sharp debridement of callus and necrotic tissue: converts a chronic wound to an acute one**), **moist wound healing**, **negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT: after debridement, post-amputation wounds)**, adjuncts (**hyperbaric oxygen (selected ischaemic wounds)**, **growth factors (becaplermin: PDGF)**, skin substitutes, **sucrose octasulfate dressings**).
- **Revascularisation** (**endovascular angioplasty or bypass**) for PAD before definitive surgery.
- **Infection:**
  - **Mild: oral antibiotics (covering gram-positive cocci) 1-2 weeks.**
  - **Moderate/severe: urgent surgical drainage/debridement (abscess, necrotising infection, gas, compartment involvement) + IV broad-spectrum antibiotics**; **"diabetic foot attack" = emergency**.
  - **Osteomyelitis:** **surgical resection of infected bone** (**± 1-3 weeks antibiotics after complete resection with clean margins**) or **prolonged antibiotics alone (6 weeks) in selected forefoot cases**.
- **Glycaemic control, nutrition, smoking cessation, renal optimisation.**

## 5. Surgical procedures
- **Prophylactic/corrective ("elective, curative, emergent" classification):**
  - **Achilles tendon lengthening (percutaneous Hoke)/gastrocnemius recession**: **forefoot plantar ulcers** (**reduces forefoot pressure: lowers recurrence (about 75% reduction at 2 years, Mueller)**: **transfer ulcers to the heel (overlengthening)**),
  - **Flexor tenotomy (percutaneous)** for **apical/tip ulcers of claw toes**,
  - **Metatarsal head resection (single or panmetatarsal)**, **sesamoidectomy**, **exostectomy** (Charcot rocker-bottom prominences), **hallux IPJ arthroplasty (Keller) for plantar hallux ulcers**.
- **Amputations (level by perfusion, function, soft-tissue coverage):**
  - **Toe/ray amputation**: **hallux amputation: transfer pressure to the lesser metatarsals**; **second toe amputation: hallux valgus**; **ray amputation (single lateral rays tolerated; first ray amputation: poor)**.
  - **Transmetatarsal amputation (TMA)**: good function; **balance with Achilles lengthening and tibialis anterior/peroneal considerations** (equinovarus deformity tendency).
  - **Lisfranc/Chopart amputations**: **equinus and varus deformity** (**tibialis anterior/posterior unopposed; Achilles unopposed**): **Achilles tenotomy + tibialis anterior transfer to the talar neck/lateral**.
  - **Syme amputation** (ankle disarticulation with **heel pad preserved and anchored to the tibia**; **heel pad migration**: commonest complication; end-bearing; needs a patent posterior tibial artery).
  - **Below-knee (transtibial) amputation (BKA)**: **preserve knee: energy expenditure about 10-40% above normal (BKA) vs about 60-100% (AKA)**; **long posterior myocutaneous flap (Burgess)**; **ideal tibial length about 12-15 cm below the joint line (about 2.5 cm per 30 cm of height)**; **fibula 1-2 cm shorter than the tibia**.
  - **Through-knee/above-knee**: non-ambulators, failed BKA, fixed knee contracture.
- **Minimum requirements for healing:** **ABI over about 0.45**, **toe pressures over about 30-40 mmHg**, **TcPO2 over 30-40 mmHg**, **serum albumin over 3.0 g/dL**, **total lymphocyte count over 1,500/µL**.

## 6. Prevention
- **Annual foot screening for all diabetics** (**monofilament, vibration, pulses, deformity, skin, footwear**); **risk stratification** (IWGDF 0-3).
- **Education (daily self-inspection, never barefoot, moisturise, nail care)**, **therapeutic footwear/insoles** (**extra-depth shoes, custom insoles**: prevent recurrence), **podiatry (callus removal)**, **temperature monitoring (home: differences over 2.2 C between feet = impending ulcer or Charcot)**.

# Part B: Charcot neuroarthropathy

## 7. Definition and pathogenesis
- **Progressive, non-infectious, destructive inflammatory process of bones and joints in a neuropathic foot**, leading to **fragmentation, dislocation, collapse and deformity**.
- **Causes:** **diabetes (commonest today, about 0.1-0.4% of diabetics; up to about 13% of high-risk)**, **leprosy (India)**, **syringomyelia (upper limb: shoulder/elbow)**, **tabes dorsalis (syphilis: knee, hip)** (historical commonest), **alcoholic neuropathy, spinal cord injury, congenital insensitivity to pain, myelomeningocele (ankle)**.
- **Theories:**
  - **Neurotraumatic (German) theory**: **repetitive unperceived microtrauma in an insensate foot**,
  - **Neurovascular (French) theory**: **autonomic neuropathy: hyperaemia (AV shunting), osteoclastic bone resorption, osteopenia**,
  - **Unifying modern theory: RANKL-OPG pathway**: **trauma triggers uncontrolled inflammation (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6): increased RANKL, osteoclast activation**; **loss of protective pain response** allows continued loading.

## 8. Eichenholtz stages (natural history) (+ Shibata stage 0)
| Stage | Name | Clinical | Radiographs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0 (Shibata, "prodromal/at-risk")** | **Inflammation** | **Warm, swollen, red foot after minor trauma** | **Normal (MRI: bone marrow oedema, microfractures)** |
| **I** | **Development (fragmentation)** | **Warm (over 2 C higher), swollen, erythematous; may be painless** | **Fragmentation, debris, joint subluxation/dislocation, osteopenia** |
| **II** | **Coalescence** | **Decreased warmth/swelling** | **Absorption of debris, sclerosis, early fusion of fragments** |
| **III** | **Reconstruction (consolidation)** | **No warmth; stable (possibly deformed) foot** | **Remodelling, bony ankylosis, deformity (rocker-bottom)** |
- **Each stage lasts months; the whole process about 1-2 years**.
- **Erythema that resolves on elevation (Brodsky elevation test: within about 1 minute)** suggests **Charcot rather than infection** (cellulitis does not resolve on elevation).

## 9. Anatomical classification (Brodsky; modified)
| Type | Region | Frequency | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Midfoot: tarsometatarsal (Lisfranc) and naviculocuneiform joints** | **Commonest (about 60-70%)** | **Rocker-bottom deformity with plantar ulceration (cuboid or medial cuneiform prominence)**; relatively stable |
| **2** | **Hindfoot: subtalar, talonavicular, calcaneocuboid (Chopart)** | **About 10-30%** | **Instability; long time to consolidate** |
| **3A** | **Ankle (tibiotalar)** | **About 10%** | **Most unstable; varus/valgus; ulceration over malleoli; worst prognosis** |
| **3B** | **Calcaneal tuberosity (pathological avulsion fracture)** | Rare | **Loss of push-off, flatfoot** |
| (**4**) | **Multiple regions** | | |
| (**5**) | **Forefoot (MTPJs)** | | |
- **Sanders and Frykberg classification (patterns I-V):** **I forefoot (MTPJ/IPJ)**, **II tarsometatarsal (Lisfranc)**, **III naviculocuneiform/TN/CC (Chopart)**, **IV ankle/subtalar**, **V calcaneus**.
- **Rogers and Bevilacqua classification:** **anatomical location (1 forefoot, 2 midfoot, 3 hindfoot/ankle)** + **A no deformity, B deformity, C ulcer, D osteomyelitis**.

## 10. Diagnosis
- **Hot, swollen foot in a neuropathic diabetic: Charcot until proved otherwise** (often **misdiagnosed as cellulitis, gout, DVT or sprain**).
- **Temperature difference over 2 C** (infrared thermometry) vs contralateral foot.
- **Radiographs (weight-bearing):** **fragmentation, dislocation, rocker-bottom (loss of calcaneal pitch, negative lateral talo-first metatarsal angle)**, **lateral column collapse**.
- **MRI** (stage 0: marrow oedema, microfractures).
- **Charcot vs osteomyelitis (key distinction):**
| Feature | **Charcot** | **Osteomyelitis** |
|---|---|---|
| Location | **Midfoot (joints, periarticular)**, multiple joints | **Forefoot or calcaneus (adjacent to ulcers)**; usually single bone |
| Ulcer | **Often absent** (or over a bony prominence) | **Ulcer contiguous with the bone; probe to bone positive** |
| Erythema | **Resolves with elevation** | Persists |
| MRI | **Subchondral/periarticular oedema; preserved fat; "ghost sign" absent** | **Diffuse marrow replacement (low T1), sinus tract, abscess; "ghost sign" (bone disappears on T1 and reappears on post-contrast)** |
| Nuclear medicine | **Labelled leucocyte scan: mild uptake** (marrow) | **Intense uptake on labelled leucocyte scan** (combined with marrow scan) |
| Gold standard | | **Bone biopsy** |

## 11. Management
### Acute phase (stage 0/I): non-operative is the mainstay
- **Immobilisation and offloading: total contact cast (TCC)** (**changed weekly initially, then every 1-2 weeks**; **non-weight bearing or protected weight bearing**) until **temperature difference falls under 2 C** (stage II/III: **about 3-6 months or longer**).
- **Then: Charcot restraint orthotic walker (CROW)** (**about 6-12 months**), then **custom footwear/AFO** (lifelong).
- **Bisphosphonates/calcitonin: no proven benefit on outcomes** (may reduce markers/temperature; not routine).
- **Monitor the contralateral foot** (**bilateral involvement in about 25-30%**).
### Surgery
- **Indications:** **unstable/unbraceable deformity**, **recurrent/non-healing ulceration over bony prominences despite offloading**, **osteomyelitis**, **progressive deformity**, **pain/instability (ankle Charcot)**.
- **Timing:** **traditionally in the coalescence/consolidation (stage II-III) phase**; **early surgery in stage I** increasingly accepted for unstable patterns (ankle) with **"superconstruct" fixation**.
- **Procedures:**
  - **Exostectomy** (**plantar bony prominence: medial column (medial cuneiform) prominences do better than lateral column (cuboid)**) for **stable deformities with ulcers**,
  - **Achilles lengthening/gastrocnemius recession** (reduces midfoot load; corrects equinus driving collapse),
  - **Reconstruction (realignment arthrodesis):**
    - **Midfoot: medial column beam (solid bolt through the first metatarsal into the talus), lateral column beams, plantar plating (tension side)**,
    - **Hindfoot/ankle: tibiotalocalcaneal (TTC) arthrodesis with a retrograde IM nail**, **circular (Ilizarov) external fixation** (**infection/osteomyelitis, poor bone, ulcers**),
    - **"Superconstruct" principles (Sammarco):** **extend fusion beyond the zone of injury to include unaffected joints**, **bony resection to shorten and decompress soft tissues**, **strongest device tolerated by soft tissue**, **devices applied in the position of maximum mechanical function (plantar plating)**,
  - **Two-stage management with infection** (**resection of infected bone, antibiotic spacer, external fixation, then definitive fusion**),
  - **Amputation (BKA)** for **recurrent ulceration/infection, failed reconstruction** (**can give better function than repeated salvage attempts**).
- **Complications:** **non-union (fibrous union may be stable and acceptable)**, **infection**, **hardware failure**, **recurrence**, **contralateral Charcot (from increased load)**, **amputation (about 5-15%)**, **mortality**.

> Exam pearl: **Neuropathy (10-g monofilament) causes most ulcers; ABI falsely high in calcified vessels: use toe pressures/TBI/TcPO2. Wagner 0-5 (3 = abscess/osteomyelitis, 4 forefoot gangrene); UT grade + stage (stage predicts amputation). Probe-to-bone; MRI best imaging; bone biopsy gold standard.**

> Exam pearl: **TCC gold standard offloading (not with infection/ischaemia). Achilles lengthening reduces forefoot ulcer recurrence (transfer heel ulcers). BKA energy cost much lower than AKA. Healing: ABI over 0.45, toe pressure over 30-40, TcPO2 over 30-40, albumin over 3.0, lymphocytes over 1,500.**

> Exam pearl: **Charcot: hot swollen neuropathic foot, temp difference over 2 C, erythema resolves with elevation. Eichenholtz I fragmentation, II coalescence, III reconstruction (Shibata 0 = MRI oedema only). Midfoot (Lisfranc) commonest; ankle worst. Treat with TCC until temperature equalises, then CROW. Surgery: unstable/ulcer/infection; superconstruct; medial column beam; TTC nail/Ilizarov.**
